analysis.one_liner: Requires election spenders to disclose major donors and bars foreign-influenced corporations from campaign spending.
analysis.headline: A campaign-disclosure bill backed by 49 senators, all Democrats and independents, was referred to committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would expand the ban on foreign money in elections to US companies that are owned or controlled by foreign nationals, and require corporations, unions, super PACs, and tax-exempt groups that spend money to influence elections to publicly report anyone who gives them $10,000 or more. Ads on TV, radio, and the internet would have to name their biggest funders. It never got past a committee referral in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would learn who is actually paying for the political ads they see; candidates and campaigns competing against undisclosed outside spending; and the public interest in keeping foreign money out of US elections.

how_it_helps.text: Expands the existing ban on foreign election spending to domestic corporations in which foreign nationals own or control at least 5% of voting shares if a foreign government is the owner, or 20% for other foreign owners, or that have foreign nationals directing their US election activity; corporate CEOs must certify compliance with the foreign-money ban under penalty of perjury before their company spends on a federal election.

Requires any corporation, labor organization, super PAC, or tax-exempt group (like 501(c)(4) nonprofits) that spends more than $10,000 on campaign ads or transfers money for that purpose to file a disclosure within 24 hours, listing every person who gave $10,000 or more and identifying the beneficial owners behind shell entities.

Extends 'stand by your ad' disclaimers to internet audio and video and to prerecorded robocalls, and requires video ads paid for with such money to display a list of their top five funders and audio ads their top two.

Repeals three appropriations provisions from the 2018 spending law that restricted the use of certain government funds, and speeds up the definition window for reportable 'electioneering communications' so election ads are covered starting January 1 of the election year.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, unions, trade associations, super PACs, and 'dark money' nonprofits that currently spend on elections without revealing their funders would have to open their books; the bill also imposes compliance costs on any group running election ads.

drawbacks.text: Donor disclosure can expose the people behind political giving to public pressure or retaliation; opponents have long argued this chills legitimate participation, and the bill's exceptions for people who give less than $10,000 narrow but do not eliminate that concern.

The bill creates substantial compliance obligations — CEO certifications under penalty of perjury, 24-hour filing deadlines, beneficial-owner tracking through shell entities — which would fall hardest on smaller organizations even as its thresholds are designed to spare small donors.

The expanded definition of what counts as 'express advocacy' and of the electioneering window would sweep in more communications, raising the risk that groups issue-targeted political speech and pull back from issue advocacy altogether.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For voters, the benefit is knowing who funds the political ads aimed at them and a stronger bar against foreign money — a direct check on undisclosed influence over elections. The costs are real but ordinary: compliance work for spending groups and a risk of harassment for disclosed large donors, a tradeoff Congress has debated since the original DISCLOSE Act. On balance the bill asks spenders for transparency in exchange for continuing to spend, which is a light price for a heavier public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee took no action on it for the rest of the Congress, so it never came to a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on June 27, 2018 with 48 cosponsors — 46 Democrats and both independents — for a total of 49 Senate supporters, all from one side of the aisle.

The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration; the action history shows no markup, hearing, floor debate, or vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
Because the Congress ended, the bill died and the same proposal would have to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

The bill's provisions — extending the foreign-money ban to foreign-influenced US corporations and requiring donor disclosure by major election spenders — never took effect, and undisclosed election spending remained the law of the land.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The groups the bill would have forced to reveal their funders — corporations, unions, trade associations, and tax-exempt nonprofits spending on elections without disclosure — are better off, since they kept the status quo of spending without naming names, and the senators opposed to or uninterested in disclosure faced no vote on it.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the DISCLOSE Act of 2018 in the Senate.

against.name: Sen. Roy Blunt
against.role: Chair, Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled any committee action on the bill, which sat without a hearing or markup until the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor and has long opposed mandated donor-disclosure requirements.

sides.party_line_note: All 49 supporters were Democrats or independents and no Republican cosponsored; with Republicans holding 51 Senate seats and controlling the Rules Committee and the floor calendar, the bill went no further than a referral.

industries.industry: Corporations and trade associations spending on elections
industries.note: The bill would force them to report donors of $10,000 or more and certify they are not spending foreign money, ending their ability to influence elections anonymously. Their current interest is in keeping funders hidden, which runs directly against voters' interest in knowing who is behind the ads.

These groups are currently the main channel for undisclosed election spending; the bill would make them disclose their major funders like any other spender. Their advantage over transparent competitors would end.

The bill would bar companies with significant foreign ownership or control from spending on US elections and require CEO certification of compliance, closing a loophole that now lets foreign money flow through domestic corporate treasuries.

Unions are 'covered organizations' under the bill and would face the same donor-disclosure requirements as corporations. The rules are symmetric, and transparency applies to both sides of the political money fight.

industries.industry: Super PACs and political committees accepting unlimited funds
industries.note: The bill would clarify that foreign money cannot be funneled to super PACs and would require the committees and their funding accounts to report their donors. Their model depends on money moving with little visibility.

industries.industry: Broadcast, cable, and internet media platforms
industries.note: The bill extends 'stand by your ad' disclaimers to internet audio and video and to prerecorded calls, adding modest compliance work for ads these platforms carry. The effect on their business is small.
